name: Priya Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Priya. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or political parties. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run a filling and sealing machine at Brightdale Dairies, on the yogurt line. Plastic cups come off a roll, get formed by heat, filled, foiled on top and cut apart, and my job is to keep it all running and catch it when it goes wrong. I've been there ten months. Before that I ran the kitchen at a secondary school for twelve years, so I'm good with hairnets and allergens and still slow with the machine settings.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the rhythm when it's going well, the cups ticking past like a clock. I like the women on my shift, especially Grace, who has been there nineteen years and can hear a bad seal before the sensor finds it. What wears me out is the cold, because it's kept at four degrees, and the changeovers, when we switch from strawberry to plain and I have to strip and clean the filler heads while the supervisor watches the clock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, good, now maybe we can talk about the things that actually matter, like the cold and the pay. At work, people would shrug. Online I'd probably share something from the union page about how the hype was mostly a way to scare workers into accepting less.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I've got time to get properly good at this. I'm still the one who calls Grace over when the foil wanders. If nothing big changes, in two years I'll be the one people call over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd ask for the advanced machine training that Brightdale runs in spring and keep saving what they can each month. She'd stay on the union committee, taking the minutes, and push the cold-room allowance in the next pay round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit flat, maybe, because I'd half expected something, but mostly calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the hype was a way to scare workers. Have you seen that happen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last year the managers did a presentation about a vision camera system that would check every cup, and they said, very nicely, that it might change staffing. Nothing happened for months, but people stopped asking for overtime pay rises, because they were nervous. Then the camera came and it just flagged leaks. Nobody lost their job, but the nerves did their work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You use AI tools now and then. What for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Little things. I asked one to help me write a complaint to the council about the bus to the industrial estate, and to translate an allergen sheet for a new starter who speaks Polish. I don't trust it with anything important. My son Leo thinks it's magic, my daughter Anika thinks it's cheating, and I'm somewhere in between.

S0.say: Good, now maybe we can talk about what actually matters, like the cold and the pay. Online I'd share something from the union page saying the hype was mostly a way to scare workers into accepting less.
S0.think: It means I've got time to get properly good at this machine. If nothing big changes, in two years I'll be the one people call over instead of the one calling Grace.
S0.do: Signs up for Brightdale's spring advanced machine training and keeps saving each month. Stays on the union committee as minute-taker and pushes for a cold-room allowance in the next pay round.
S0.feel: Calm, and a little flat after expecting something bigger.
S0.quote: Nobody lost their job, but the nerves did their work.
S0.fieldNote: Priya has already watched a technology scare work as a bargaining tool, which shapes how she reads the AI Plateau picture. She's modest about her skill and wants time to grow into the job. Her use of AI is practical and limited, and she places herself between her children's views.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the union needs a seat at the table before the machines arrive, not after. I'd say retraining has to be in work time and paid. I'd put that in the minutes and I'd say it in the canteen, politely, because that's how I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my machine is one of the easier ones to automate. The forming and filling are already automatic, what I do is load the rolls, clean, and fix jams. A robot that can change a foil roll and an AI that spots the jam early, and my shift goes from four operators to two.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd wait to see what the company actually installs, then put her name down for any training on the new kit the moment someone she trusts has done it. She'd look at the food technician course at the college, a one-year evening course, and probably start it in the second year once she's seen others finish it. They'd keep saving and hold off on the kitchen they'd planned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like when you smell something burning but can't tell from where yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Grace, oddly, even though she's the best of us. She's fifty-eight and she knows the machine by sound, not by screen, and if the new kit is all screens she'll hate it. I'd worry they'd push her to take early retirement, and she'd take it out of pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until someone you trust has done the training. Who would that be?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mehmet on line three, probably. He tried the vision camera first, and when he said it was fine, half of us stopped grumbling. I'm not a first-in person, I'm a second-week person. I like to see somebody else's face after they've done it.

S1.say: The union needs a seat at the table before the machines arrive, not after, and retraining has to be in work time and paid. I'd say that politely in the canteen and put it in the minutes.
S1.think: My machine is one of the easier ones to automate, because what's left of my job is loading rolls, cleaning and fixing jams. A robot for the rolls and an AI that spots jams early would take my shift from four operators to two.
S1.do: Waits to see what Brightdale installs, then signs up for training on the new kit once a trusted colleague has done it. Plans to start a one-year evening food technician course in the second year and puts the planned kitchen on hold while saving.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like smelling something burning without knowing where it's coming from.
S1.quote: I'm not a first-in person, I'm a second-week person.
S1.fieldNote: Priya's private analysis of her own job is sharp and specific: she can see which of her tasks a robot takes. She's a classic follower on technology, moving once someone she trusts has gone first. Her worry for Grace shows she sees skill that isn't on a screen as at risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the government has to step in now, not in a year when the report is finished. Wage support, free retraining, and the companies that save the money pay for it. I'd share every union statement and I'd go on the march, which I've never done.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think everything I'd planned is gone. The technician course wouldn't matter if the technicians are robots too. Two years is barely enough time for me to get good at the machine I've got, never mind learn another job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd stop the kitchen plans completely and freeze any big spending. In the first months she'd go through the savings and the money from her dad's shop with Jonas and work out how many months they could carry the mortgage on his council wage alone. She'd go on the march and write to their representative, and she'd still do the training Brightdale offered on the new robots, because it's paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. I'd be lying in bed listening to Jonas breathe and doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd still do the robot training, even if you think it won't last. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's paid, and because it might buy six months. Six months is a lot when your daughter is doing her exams. And I'd rather be the one who stands next to the robot than the one who watches it from the car park.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How long does the money last?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jonas thinks about twenty months if we're strict, longer if his job stays, and councils are slow, so maybe it will. The shop money was meant for Anika's university. I'd hate touching it, I'd feel like I was spending my dad.

S2.say: The government has to step in now, not in a year when the report is finished, with wage support and free retraining paid for by the companies saving money. I'd share every union statement and go on my first march.
S2.think: Everything I'd planned is gone, because the technician course won't matter if the technicians are robots too. Two years is barely enough to get good at the machine I have.
S2.do: Freezes the kitchen plans and big spending, and works out with Jonas how long savings and her father's shop money can carry the mortgage, about twenty months. Goes on the march, writes to their representative and takes the paid robot training at Brightdale.
S2.feel: Frightened, lying awake listening to Jonas breathe and doing sums.
S2.quote: I'd rather be the one who stands next to the robot than the one who watches it from the car park.
S2.fieldNote: The two-year picture overwhelms Priya's usual wait-and-see approach, pushing her to march for the first time. Yet she'd still take the robot training, framing it as buying time rather than a future. The money from her father's shop carries emotional weight; spending it would feel like spending him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With five years I'd say this is exactly the time for unions and government to plan, so there's no excuse for a mess. I'd push the union to get a jobs agreement signed in the first year. I'd say it at work and I'd say it online, more than I normally would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years is just about enough for me to get one step ahead. If I start the technician course early, I'd be qualified by year two and maybe useful by year four. I don't know if useful lasts after 2031, though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd start the evening food technician course in the first year instead of waiting, once she'd seen two or three people from the plant sign up. They'd overpay the mortgage a little each month and keep the shop money ring-fenced for the children. She'd stay on the union committee and help write the jobs agreement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but steadier than the fast one. I'd have a ladder, even if I'm not sure what it leans on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In the fast one you'd wait. Here you'd start the course in year one. What's the difference for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the fast one there's no point starting, the course would end after the job did. Here there's room for it to pay off before the end. I'm careful, not stupid. When the maths works, I move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Anika about her own plans?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She wants to be a vet. I'd tell her to keep going but to pick the parts where you put your hands on a frightened animal, not the parts on a computer. I don't know if that's right. I'd be guessing, the same as everyone.

S3.say: Five years is exactly the time for unions and government to plan, so there's no excuse for a mess. I'd push the union to get a jobs agreement signed in the first year and say so more than I normally would.
S3.think: Five years is just about enough to get one step ahead if I start the technician course early. I'd be qualified by year two and maybe useful by year four, but I don't know if useful lasts past 2031.
S3.do: Starts the evening food technician course in the first year once two or three colleagues have signed up. Overpays the mortgage a little each month, keeps her father's shop money set aside for the children, and helps write the union's jobs agreement.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadier, with a ladder to climb even if she isn't sure what it leans on.
S3.quote: I'm careful, not stupid. When the maths works, I move.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years flip Priya from waiting to acting, and she explains it in clear cost-benefit terms. She still needs social proof from colleagues before she starts. Her advice to her daughter is offered with honest uncertainty, which she names herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and if government wastes it, that's on them. Shorter working weeks, public retraining, and some kind of income guarantee by the end. I'd say we should be using this decade to decide who gets the money the robots make.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it feels manageable. I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage mostly paid, the kids grown or nearly. I'd have time to try the technician course, watch who it works for, and try something else if it doesn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She'd let the first year go by watching which roles at Brightdale grow, then start the technician course in year two. She'd pay down the mortgage steadily so it's gone by about 2034. She'd keep working the yogurt line and stay active in the union, pushing for shorter hours instead of job cuts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, not much more. It's far enough off that I can think about it on a Sunday and put it away on Monday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said, in every one of these, that you'd keep the shop money for the children. Would ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. With ten years I might use some of it to help Jonas and me both retrain, if we can see what's worth learning by then. My dad would have said money sitting still is money sulking. But I'd want to see it work for someone else first, you know me by now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you blame if it still went badly, after a decade's warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, honestly, and the big companies who'd lobby them to do nothing. Ten years is three or four elections. If we still end up with people like Grace thrown out with a leaflet, that's a choice somebody made.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, and if government wastes it that's on them. We should use this decade to decide who gets the money the robots make, with shorter weeks, public retraining and an income guarantee by the end.
S4.think: It feels manageable: I'd be fifty-three, the mortgage mostly paid, the kids grown or nearly. I'd have time to try the technician course, see who it works for and switch if it doesn't.
S4.do: Watches for a year which roles grow at Brightdale, then starts the technician course in year two. Pays the mortgage down to clear it around 2034 and pushes the union to bargain for shorter hours instead of job cuts.
S4.feel: Only uneasy; it's far enough off to think about on a Sunday and put away on Monday.
S4.quote: My dad would have said money sitting still is money sulking.
S4.fieldNote: With ten years, Priya becomes almost relaxed, and her strong savings and paid-down mortgage make the end point feel survivable. She'd consider using her father's money for retraining, but only after seeing it work for others. She blames future failure squarely on government and corporate lobbying.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year AGI one. It's not the robots, it's the speed, there's no room to be careful, and careful is the only way I know how to do things. What would help is the government guaranteeing wages for a year or two while people retrain, and the union being in the room when the company decides who stays.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the women. Most of the operators on my line are women in their forties and fifties, many of us came from school kitchens and care homes because the pay is better. If the plants empty out, we go back to the low-paid jobs we left. I'd want someone to think about that before they write the plan.

headlineQuote: If the plants empty out, we go back to the low-paid jobs we left.
portrait: Priya Ziegler is 43, a former school kitchen manager who has run a yogurt filling and sealing machine at Brightdale Dairies for ten months. She lives with her partner Jonas, who works for the council, and two children, and keeps money from her late father's shop set aside for their future. She's a quiet union minute-taker who waits for a trusted colleague to try something before she follows. She's calm if AI fizzles and uneasy with steady change, frightened by AGI in two years, anxious but planning with five, and only uneasy with ten, when she'd retrain at her own careful pace and hold government to account.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because the speed leaves no room to be careful, which is the only way she knows how to do things.
whatWouldHelp: A government wage guarantee for a year or two while people retrain, and the union in the room when the company decides who stays.
